newsitem.title: FRANCE: Tietmeyer says believes EMU will start on time.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer says believes EMU will start on time.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said in an interview with afternoon daily Le Monde that barring surprises European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would start on time in 1999.
"There are strong reasons to believe today that the timetable will be respected, at least by a limited number of countries, as foreseen in the Maastricht treaty.
"I start from the principle that if nothing surprising happens between now and then, monetary union will begin at the start of 1999," he said.
He said the determining factor in deciding in the spring of 1998 on which countries qualify to join monetary union must be the need to ensure a lasting and solid monetary union.
"One-off results are not enough as proof of respect for the (Maastricht treaty) stability criteria," he said.
"All the figures, for example the budget figures, must be fulfilled not on the basis of a massaging of the balance sheet, but in the direction of long-term solidity," he said.
Asked whether he considered France's use of France Telecom funds to reduce its budget deficit next year as window-dressing, he said he had no intention of criticising countries by name.
But he noted that it had been France which had proposed that budget deficits be limited to three percent of gross domestic product and this had been agreed by its European partners.
"I have the impression that some people do not like to be reminded of something to which they have already given their agreement," he said.
"Naturally, there is, as regards the (Maastricht) criteria, room for interpretation which must be analysed very carefully," he said.
Europe would have to take a step back and look not just at the figures but at what was behind the figures to see whether efforts to meet Maastricht treaty criteria could be sustained.
"On one hand, the treaty names figures, but on the other, it provides room for interpretation which must, in the same way as for the figures, be read and respected strictly," he said.
